title: Conditionals
summary: A condition lets a program choose what to do. An if statement runs some code when a rule is true.
introduction: A condition lets a program choose what to do. An if statement runs some code when a rule is true. A game might say "You win" when points reach ten. Write a small rule, then test values on both sides of it.
learningObjectives: Write if, else if and else branches that cover every case
List the falsy values and predict how a condition evaluates
Use switch for a value with many fixed options
Simplify nested conditions with early returns

blocks.text: `if` runs its block when the condition in parentheses is true. `else if` adds another condition that is only checked when the previous ones were false, and `else` catches everything that is left. The branches are tested from top to bottom and exactly one runs, so order matters: put the most specific condition first.
`hour < 12` is false, so the first block is skipped. `hour < 18` is true, so the second block runs and the `else` is never reached. Change `hour` to `9` or `21` and run it again.

A condition does not have to be a boolean. JavaScript converts whatever you put inside `if (...)` to true or false. Only a handful of values convert to false; they are called **falsy**, and everything else is **truthy**. Knowing the list lets you write `if (name)` to mean 'if a name was given' and `if (items.length)` to mean 'if the list is not empty'.

`describe` is a small function so the test can be repeated; the [Functions](/tutorials/javascript/functions) lesson explains the syntax. The results to remember: the string `"0"` is truthy because it is not empty, and an empty array is truthy because it is an object. To check whether an array has items, test its `length`.

When one value is compared against a list of fixed options, a chain of `else if` gets repetitive. `switch` compares the value with each `case` using strict equality and runs the matching block. Execution continues into the next case until it meets `break`, which is how several cases can share one block, as `"sat"` and `"sun"` do below. `default` handles anything that did not match.

blocks.title: A missing break falls through
blocks.text: Without `break`, execution continues into the next case even though its value did not match. Remove the `break` after `"Weekend"` in the example and the output becomes `Weekend` followed by `Almost weekend`. Intentional fall-through (several cases sharing a block) is fine; an accidental one is a classic bug.

Deeply nested `if` blocks are hard to follow. Inside a function you can instead handle the special cases first and `return` immediately, so the remaining code deals only with the normal case. Each condition is read on its own, without remembering the ones above it.

The logical operators from the [Operators](/tutorials/javascript/operators) lesson let one `if` express several requirements. `&&` demands both, `||` accepts either, and `!` negates. For a simple choice between two values, the ternary operator is shorter than an `if`/`else`.
A mistake that looks like a comparison

A single `=` inside a condition assigns instead of comparing. The assignment evaluates to the assigned value, so `if (role = "admin")` is always truthy and quietly overwrites `role`. Run the example and notice that it prints `admin` even though the variable was `guest`. Use `===`, and consider putting the constant on the left (`"admin" === role`), which makes the typo a syntax error.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Rewrite the greeting example as a function `greeting(hour)` that uses early returns instead of else if, then call it with 9, 14 and 21. The output should not change.

questions.question: Which of these values is falsy?
questions.explanation: The falsy values are false, 0 (including -0 and 0n), "", null, undefined and NaN. The string "0", an empty array and the string "false" are all truthy.

questions.question: In a switch statement, execution continues into the next case unless it meets a break.
questions.explanation: That behaviour is called fall-through. It is useful for grouping cases, but forgetting a break runs code that was meant for another value.

seo.title: JavaScript Conditionals – if, else, switch and Truthiness
seo.description: Learn JavaScript conditionals: if, else if and else, the falsy values, switch with break and default, early returns and the assignment-in-condition bug.
